# Why is the weighted-QP WBC framework lacking the support leg static constraint?

> **Current answer:** Comment explains that the original library, aside from contact force tracking, also enforces constraints on the support legs not moving. However, the author encountered issues during debugging and removed this constraint. The current content does not provide evidence that the removal is correct in all contact scenarios, nor does it specify the exact residual constraints causing conflicts.

## Key terms

- Whole-Body Control (WBC) (全身控制)
- Quadratic Programming (QP) (二次规划)
- Model Predictive Control (MPC) (模型预测控制)
- State Estimation (状态估计)
- Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) (统一机器人描述格式)
- Joint Torque (关节力矩)

## Problem and symptoms

- How can we reduce the difficulty of diagnosing errors when migrating an open-source NMPC+WBC framework to a custom robot model?
- Why was the support leg static constraint omitted from the framework?
- After model change, the OCS2 SQP's LQ Approximation consumes 93.5% of the runtime and the dummy robot is stationary.
- The foot trajectory of the custom model is abnormally directed, and the dummy node does not respond to commands.
- A comment measures the LQ Approximation at 1528.7 ms, which accounts for 93.5049% of the total SQP time.

## Environment

- MuJoCo simulation; OCS2 NMPC; Pinocchio dynamics; qpOASES weighted-QP WBC; SolidWorks export of URDF.

## Priority diagnostics

- Isolated the MPC using an OCS2 dummy, then used the Cheat Controller to read simulation truth values and isolate the state estimator.
- Checked the inertial properties of the URDF, foot kinematic constraints, and the weighted-QP H matrix weights.

## Possible causes

- The inertia matrix exported by the SolidWorks URDF plugin may be incorrect.
- The support leg static constraint was removed during debugging due to issues, and the SQP linearization bottleneck remains unconfirmed.

## Attempts

- The author first completed the Cheat Controller, then added and stabilized the linear Kalman state estimator.
- Re-filled the inertia using SolidWorks quality attributes according to the link coordinate system and negative tensor notation.

## Effective fixes

- Used a layered validation approach: dummy → Cheat Controller → state estimator, and corrected the inertia parameters.

## Result

- The original author reported that the simulation framework can run stably; the support leg constraint and linearization of the SQP are not fully resolved in the final version.

## Limitations

- Primary evidence comes from simulation and the comment section; no independent validation in real humanoid robots or high-speed motion has been provided.

## Safety notes

- Incorrect inertial parameters, contact constraints, or state estimation should not be directly deployed on real machines; they should be validated in dummy and simulation first.
